content: The term vaccine critic refers to individuals whose stance on vaccination is not entirely oppositional but is nuanced and specific. These individuals may advocate against certain aspects of vaccination, such as a single component of a particular vaccine, for reasons that are specific to that component. They are distinct from outright anti-vaccinationists, who oppose all forms of vaccination. Some vaccine critics may describe themselves as such while actively campaigning to prevent or avoid specific vaccinations under particular circumstances. This group includes individuals who support certain immunizations for specific populations in defined situations, provided they clearly articulate their reasoning. In contrast, anti-vaccinationists are those who oppose vaccination in its entirety. They often identify themselves as critics but fundamentally reject the practice of immunization as a whole. The distinction between vaccine critics and anti-vaccinationists has been explored in academic literature, such as a 2005 review in the Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine. This review examined the differences between modern anti-vaccination campaigns and those that existed prior to 1907. It also highlighted the importance of differentiating vaccine critics, who may support some immunizations, from anti-vaccinationists, who reject all vaccines. Prominent vaccine critics include Neil Z. Miller, Alan Cantwell, and Edward Yazbak. On the other hand, notable anti-vaccinationists include organizations like the National Anti-Vaccination League and individuals such as Gerhard Buchwald, Robert S. Mendelsohn, Viera Scheibner, Charles Creighton, Beddow Bayly, and Hans Rüesch. For further historical context, Nadja Durbach’s 2005 book Bodily Matters: The Anti-Vaccination Movement in England, 1853–1907 provides an in-depth exploration of the anti-vaccination movement during that period.
